title: AI adoption is outrunning public trust, formal preparation and confidence in shared economic gains
source_unit: SCSP-Gallup, American AI Sentiment in 2026, September 16, 2026
geography: United States; adults aged 18 and older

observations.period: June 2-23, 2026 survey; use, knowledge and trust

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Gallup Panel survey

use_at_least_sometimes.unit: percent using AI at least sometimes at work, school or in personal life

knowledgeable.unit: percent describing themselves as very or somewhat knowledgeable about AI

trust_fair_unbiased.unit: percent who fully or somewhat trust AI to make fair and unbiased decisions

observations.method: SCSP-Gallup nationally representative probability-based Gallup Panel web survey conducted June 2-23, 2026; weighted to the U.S. adult population.
observations.uncertainty: Use, knowledge and trust are self-reported and the trust question concerns fair and unbiased decisions rather than all possible AI uses; the survey does not measure verified usage, system performance or longitudinal behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with age and frequency-of-use comparisons in the report.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher use may increase familiarity without increasing confidence in high-stakes or consequential decisions; stable aggregate trust can also conceal divergent user and non-user trajectories.

observations.period: June 2-23, 2026 survey; use experience and trust gradient

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Gallup Panel survey

regular_user_trust.unit: percent of people using AI sometimes or more who trust it to make fair and unbiased decisions

rare_or_nonuser_trust.unit: percent of people using AI rarely or never who express the same trust

use_trust_gap.unit: percentage-point descriptive difference between regular users and rare/nonusers

trust_intervention_preferences.value: Greater company transparency, independent expert testing and pre-deployment fairness testing receive 49%, 48% and 46% support respectively as trust-building measures.

observations.method: Gallup comparison of trust by reported AI-use frequency and responses to possible trust-building interventions.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-sectional difference cannot determine whether use builds trust, trusting people use more, or both reflect education, occupation, age, access and perceived stakes.
observations.subgroup: Adults using AI sometimes or more versus rarely or never.
observations.counterinterpretation: Experience may create calibrated trust for low-stakes tasks while increasing concern about fairness and accountability in high-stakes decisions.

observations.period: June 2-23, 2026 survey; economic expectations and transition security

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Gallup Panel survey

reduce_growth.unit: percent expecting AI to reduce U.S. economic growth

boost_growth.unit: percent expecting AI to boost U.S. economic growth

destroy_more_jobs.unit: percent expecting AI to destroy more jobs than it creates over the next decade

replacement_retraining_confidence.unit: percent expecting most or all workers whose jobs are replaced to learn new skills for different work

workplace_productivity_positive.unit: percent expecting AI to have a positive impact on workplace productivity

observations.method: Descriptive survey estimates of expected AI effects on growth, jobs, business creation/destruction, productivity and retraining.
observations.uncertainty: These are expectations, not forecasts or observed labor-market outcomes; the report does not estimate job transitions, wage changes, productivity measurement or who captures gains.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with younger-adult pessimism highlighted in the report.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may distinguish aggregate productivity from distributive security: AI can improve workplace output while still being expected to reduce jobs or leave displaced workers without a credible bridge.

observations.period: June 2-23, 2026 survey; informal learning and bipartisan preparation preferences

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Gallup Panel survey

asked_ai_for_ai_help.unit: percent who asked an AI for help with using or understanding AI

asked_human_for_ai_help.unit: percent who asked another human for help with using or understanding AI

online_training.unit: percent completing online AI training videos or articles

support_stem.unit: percent supporting STEM education to equip workers with AI skills

support_on_the_job_training.unit: percent supporting on-the-job AI training programs

support_safety_over_speed.unit: percent saying government should prioritize safety and data-security rules even if development slows

support_independent_testing.unit: percent saying independent experts should test AI safety before wide use

observations.method: Descriptive survey estimates of self-directed learning and policy preferences; the report notes similar training support across party groups.
observations.uncertainty: Stated support does not establish willingness to fund, complete or use training, nor agreement about curriculum, testing standards, institutional authority or enforcement.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with party comparisons for selected policy proposals.
observations.counterinterpretation: Self-teaching may be a practical access route rather than institutional rejection, but the gap between informal use and formal preparation can leave responsibility for safe adoption on individuals.

boundary: This record adds a public-legitimacy and preparation mechanism: AI use and informal learning are expanding faster than trust, formal training, perceived economic security and institutional testing. The survey does not establish actual AI performance, labor-market displacement, causal trust change, training effectiveness, policy implementation or future economic outcomes.
